chunks: My father (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: Sa'd ibn Abd Allah narrated: Muhammad ibn 'Isa narrated, from Isma'il ibn Sahl, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

I said: 'Does Allah always know?' He said: 'How can He know when there is nothing to be known?' I said: 'Does Allah always hear?' He said: 'How can He hear when there is nothing to be heard?' I said: 'Does He always see?' He said: 'How can He see when there is nothing to be seen?' Then he said: 'Allah has always been All-Knowing, All-Hearing, All-Seeing, possessing knowledge, hearing, and seeing.'

key_terms.مَسْمُوعٌ: The heard / That which is heard
key_terms.مَعْلُومٌ: The known / That which is known
key_terms.مُبْصِرٌ: The seen / That which is seen

ai.seo_question: How does Shia theology explain the eternity of Allah's knowledge versus the temporality of the created world?
ai.summary: In this narration from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *al-Tawhid*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the doctrine of *Sifat al-Dhat* (Essential Attributes) by linking Allah’s eternal knowledge, hearing, and sight to the necessity of their respective objects (*ma'lum*, *masmi*, *mubtir*). This highlights the Shia theological distinction that while the attributes themselves are co-eternal with the Divine Essence, their actualization depends on the existence of the created realm, avoiding both anthropomorphism and total negation. The Imam’s concluding phrase emphasizes that these attributes are intrinsic to God’s self, not accidental additions, affirming the unity of essence and attribute in a manner consistent with the school of al-Kulayni and al-Saduq.
